Programming doesn't pigeon hole you into anything. Programming is useful for just about any career aside from manual labor. For instance though I'm a software engineer my wife is an educator. You end up writing the same report with little more than a different selection from a pool of adjectives and phrases hundreds of times. One easy solution - automate it. Check a box on student characteristics, slide a bar indicating levels, and write a program to generate the report which you can then edit if desired and end doing it all in about 1% of the time. No, for a variety of reasons.

  • Formalized schooling is often optimized to crush the joy of learning and turn it into an endless cycle of endure, regurgitate, repeat, forget. That isn't going to work well with programming. You alienate a lot of people who would be interested in it by turning what should be joyful into a burden. Programming requires some level of real interest to write any code that's worth much. Even people who are professional programmers who now hate the entire practice usually had interest in it at one time, which is enough to let them remain (hopefully) competent.

  • In a lot of ways, you either have the talent for writing code, or you don't. Programming bends your mind in funny ways at times, and that doesn't happen easily for people who have the right mental inclination. Although there are exceptions who will push through it and manage to become good programmers despite this, for the most part, if you don't have it, you're going to lock up fairly early on and become extremely frustrated, and possibly flunk a subject you didn't want to take in the first place. I don't think that's a fair thing to foist on a kid, especially when you can do a lot of useful things in society that do not involve writing any code. I suspect that it will remain that way for a very long time, especially since eventually AI interfaces will be a lot more oriented towards natural language. In fact, that will only further solidify the gap between the masses, who use natural language exclusively, and professional developers, who actually write programs. In the meantime, we get hacks who ignore simple things like sanitizing input, resulting in massive hacks we hear about these days. You want to see your bank account ripped open because someone never uses, for instance, a SQLSanitizeString() function? Because this is a fantastic way to get SQL injection attack points.

  • You are probably not going to be getting a whole lot of useful programming skill out of it anyway. Most useful programming is going to require knowing a language (which may or may not be standard and may or may not be easily acquired) along with knowledge of the specific system (e.g. Excel, Win32 API, POSIX, etc.) and knowledge of how that system WORKS. And that's only to get basic utility. You're going to need to actually understand the problem, and the logic, that goes into it well enough to be able to write a program that is actually an effective solution. All too often, even professional programmers only have time and knowledge to cobble something together that kinda-sorta works and limps along just well enough. Worse yet, someday someone is going to need to maintain that code. I don't know how many of you have heard of the legends of ancient COBOL programs that power a lot of businesses today on mainframes all over the world. These programs, or so I am told, are in many cases the result of having an endless stream of programmers (usually not trained) fixing and changing things with little regard for the future, and as a result, after 20 years of this, the company's very life depends on these programs but nobody knows a thing about how they really work. This is an extremely undesirable situation. It's bad enough when you have good code - that can be hard to follow in itself. Even professional programmers usually have very bad habits. Having people who are totally untrained throwing in jury-rigged algorithms is a recipe for disaster, especially considering we rely on computers even more now.

  • The prior points are compounded by the fact that you are not going to have a professional programmer doing the teaching for this, you're going to get whoever was "good with computers" that works at the school that has a teaching accreditation, or each teacher will have to do it by themselves for their own class. Elementary school teachers are a crapshoot, ranging from "good" to "complete shit that should probably be in jail." Even the good ones may not have a head for code and may struggle (at best) to teach this. Having these people teaching programming is going to go far in making sure that at least some significant chunk of the students have a fantastic start at writing shitty code. Of course, that assumes that the students can produce functioning code at all; in a really bad case of this they have conceptual damage that has to actively be undone before they can write anything that runs that's more sophisticated than Hello World.

  • This is mostly from memories from a long time ago, but I remember years and years ago there was a study noting that kids were not mentally developed enough to really get programming (at least, object oriented programming) until they were in their early to mid teens, or possibly even a little later. While I take this with a grain of salt, especially since a lot of good programmers cut their teeth on Apple II BASIC while in Kindergarten, I can't help but think that the average student is going to get even less out of a programming class in elementary school because of this.

  • As a side note, while I can understand this being taught in an effort to let kids know "how computers work," I can't help but wonder if "intro to programming" is really going to be enough. Learning how to write BASIC is not, for instance, going to teach you about how programs interact, about multithreading or multitasking, or anything else about how computers REALLY work these days. Personally I think this will PROBABLY help with that particular aspect to some extent (which may be the ONLY thing it helps with), there are going to be major gaps, and filling those gaps can cause some rather serious difficulties.

Now, an elective class would be one thing. But AFAIK there are no electives in elementary school, so everyone will have to stick their face into it. Ultimately I don't think that's going to help anyone. At the very least this should be done after elementary school, and I think that anyone who is in favor of this should look long and hard at what actual benefit it provides. Probably very little, since I doubt most will have the knowledge of where to go for that domain knowledge, or the patience to wade through documentation to find things. Most of those who do it anyway (e.g. that one guy in the office that's a whiz with Excel formulas and Word macros) would do it whether or not they had a class; in fact, they may be more likely to do it because they had no class to ruin their experience with programming beforehand.
